Second Great Awakening
SEK-uhnd grayt uh-WAY-kuhn-ing
proper noun
From second + great awakening; the American revival movement of roughly 1790–1840.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Second Great Awakening was a wave of religious revival that swept the American frontier and the established churches from roughly 1790 into the 1840s, marked by camp meetings, fervent preaching, and a great increase of professed conversions, voluntary societies, and missionary and reform labor. Genuine grace was at work in much of it: many were truly converted, churches were planted on the frontier, and the energies of awakened believers flowed into Bible societies, missions, and works of mercy. Yet the movement is a mixed inheritance, for alongside the true work ran a corrupting theology, most visibly in Charles Finney, who denied the Reformed doctrines of human inability and sovereign regeneration and taught that revival is not a miracle of God but the right use of means—the result of a properly worked-up excitement. This man-centered method, with its new measures, sowed seeds of the decisionism and emotional manipulation that have plagued American evangelicalism since. The dictionary distinguishes the true work of the Spirit, who quickens whom He will, from the Pelagianizing theology that learned to manufacture its counterfeit, and tests every awakening by its fruit and its doctrine, that the church may rejoice in the one and refuse the other.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

American revival movement (c. 1790–1840); genuine grace mixed with the man-centered revivalism of Finney, whose new measures sowed decisionism.

SECOND GREAT AWAKENING, American revival movement, c. 1790–1840.

Camp meetings, frontier preaching, and a great increase of professed conversions.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Awakening is idealized as a pure outpouring or dismissed as mere emotionalism; the truth distinguishes the real work of the Spirit from Finney’s man-centered counterfeit.

expand to see more

The corrupting theology of the Second Great Awakening is most sharply seen in Charles Finney, who taught that the new birth is not a sovereign work of God upon a dead and unable sinner but the natural result of rightly applied means—that revival could be produced by men as a crop is produced by farming. This is a denial of the plain word that men are born not of the will of man but of God (John 1:13), and that the wind of the Spirit blows where it lists (John 3:8). Finney’s new measures—the anxious bench, the protracted meeting engineered for effect—trained generations to mistake aroused emotion for regeneration.

Yet the answer to Finney’s error is not to dismiss the whole season as mere emotionalism, for God truly converted many and truly advanced His church through it. The dictionary therefore divides the spoil: it rejoices in the genuine work of the Spirit, who gave the increase (1 Cor 3:6), and it refuses the Pelagianizing method that learned to manufacture a counterfeit. Every awakening is to be tried by its doctrine and its fruit. Where men are truly humbled, brought to Christ, and made holy, God is at work; where excitement is engineered and inability denied, the work is of man, and will not stand.

Second + Great Awakening; the American revival of c. 1790–1840, genuine grace mixed with Finney’s man-centered revivalism.
